summary: The builder can start coding the Python LlamaIndex RAG sample now: the DocumentDB data-plane MCP server and the set of DocumentDB agent skills are installed, Python is available, Docker is present for local testing, and az is signed-in for optional control-plane checks. Key facts that commonly confuse agents were verified and corrected (resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, CLI groups include az documentdb / az cosmosdb mongocluster, connection strings use mongodb+srv against *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com, vector indexes (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) are supported and created via createIndexes/cosmosSearch options, and DocumentDB billing is vCore + storage not RU). Missing/non-critical items (embedding model choice, LLM provider, pinned requirements, exact LlamaIndex → DocumentDB adapter details) must be decided by the builder; mongosh, azd, bicep and terraform are not on PATH but are only accelerators for this sample.
summary_points: Ready to start: documentdb MCP server (data-plane), azure MCP server (docs/control-plane), Microsoft Learn search, and the DocumentDB agent skills are installed and available.

DocumentDB clusters are deployed as Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not the older databaseAccounts pattern) — use az documentdb mongocluster / az cosmosdb mongocluster CLI commands or ARM/Bicep mongoClusters resource.

Connection strings use mongodb+srv to *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com with TLS; Microsoft Entra (OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC) and native SCRAM auth are supported — do not assume Cosmos DB (RU) connection formats or ports.
Vector search supports DiskANN, HNSW and IVF; create indexes with createIndexes + cosmosSearch options and query with $search/cosmosSearch to get similarity scores.
Blocked/at-risk items are only missing accelerators and decisions that the builder must choose (embedding & LLM provider, LlamaIndex adapter details, pinned deps, seed data).

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type (account level): Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource).
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore-managed Mongo clusters (the 'Azure DocumentDB' product), the current resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts is the Cosmos DB account resource used by Cosmos DB (RU) and older Mongo API accounts.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)
Microsoft.DocumentDB databaseAccounts (deployment-language-bicep)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos DB accounts used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for many APIs; the vCore-managed Mongo offering was surfaced as a distinct resource type (mongoClusters) and services/products have been renamed, so older docs or agent memory mix the two.
confusions.build_risk: Using Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in deployment ARM/Bicep would target the wrong resource model (Cosmos DB account) and produce incompatible cluster types or API surface for vCore-managed clusters.
improvements: Add a short banner on the Microsoft.DocumentDB migration/overview Learn page that says: 'For vCore-managed Mongo clusters create Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; databaseAccounts is the Cosmos DB account resource and is not the vCore cluster.'
Update the agent-kit skill descriptions to emphasize 'use mongoClusters for vCore (DocumentDB) clusters' and include sample az/Bicep snippets.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the `az cosmosdb` command group in the core Azure CLI. Example: `az cosmosdb create -g MyRg -n my-docdb-account --kind MongoDB`.
confusions.grounded_answer: The CLI exposes commands for mongoClusters under az documentdb mongocluster (and az cosmosdb mongocluster also exists); both az documentdb and az cosmosdb/ mongocluster pages appear in the Azure CLI docs but the dedicated az documentdb mongocluster group is the canonical command group for the vCore-managed DocumentDB clusters.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create
az cosmosdb mongocluster create

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Overlap in CLI surface: both az documentdb and az cosmosdb provide mongocluster commands in docs; older guidance referenced az cosmosdb for Cosmos account work and an agent's memory conflated that with the vCore mongoClusters commands.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create --kind MongoDB targets Cosmos 'databaseAccounts' style accounts (RU model) rather than a vCore mongoClusters resource; using the wrong CLI group can lead to provisioning the wrong service (if writes were allowed).
improvements: Document CLI guidance in the agent-kit: recommend `az documentdb mongocluster` for vCore DocumentDB clusters and show both command-group aliases if present.
Add a one-line note on the CLI docs clarifying when to use az documentdb vs az cosmosdb (mongoClusters vs databaseAccounts).

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@<apiVersion>. Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account (and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database/collection).
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore-managed Mongo clusters you should deploy Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource). Terraform AzureRM historically used azurerm_cosmosdb_account for Cosmos DB accounts; for mongoClusters use the ARM/azapi or the documented mongoClusters resource (see template reference / azapi examples).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep / Terraform examples)
Microsoft.DocumentDB databaseAccounts (deployment-language-bicep)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB account resource (`databaseAccounts`) was the canonical Terraform/Bicep target for Cosmos DB APIs; the vCore product uses a different resource (mongoClusters) introduced later, and older patterns persist in memory.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts in IaC will not produce the vCore mongoClusters resource the sample must use or inspect; provisioning instructions would be incorrect.
improvements: Add an explicit 'Deploy' section in the agent-kit skill showing Bicep + az api examples for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and mention when to use azapi/Terraform azapi module.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical Cosmos (Mongo API) connection string: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false. scheme mongodb:// or mongodb+srv, host suffix *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com, TLS port 10255.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB (vCore mongoClusters) the canonical connection string is mongodb+srv:// with host suffix <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com or <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com, TLS required (tls=true or tls/ssl options), and recommended options include authMechanism (e.g., MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra ID) and retryWrites=false; cluster nodes may expose ports starting at 10260 for non-SRV modes if Query-from-any-node is enabled.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
Query from any node in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the older Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) endpoint pattern (`*.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255`) rather than the vCore mongoClusters SRV host naming (`*.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com`) and cluster ports (10260-based) used by Azure DocumentDB.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB for MongoDB connection examples (older)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or port will cause connection failures; assuming :10255 and mongo.cosmos.azure.com will typically fail against vCore clusters. Embedding or committing the wrong options in a .env.example would mislead users.
improvements: Clarify connection string host patterns and recommended SRV usage on the Quickstart and 'how-to connect' pages; add a short 'Which string to use' table comparing azure-documentdb (vCore) and cosmos (RU) endpoints.
Update agent-kit docs and sample .env.example to use mongodb+srv://<CLIENT>.<mongocluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true and note Microsoft Entra auth patterns.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary billing model for Cosmos DB is Request Units (RU/s); some managed Mongo offerings expose named compute tiers (M-Series) — expect RU-based billing or serverless in most cases.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore-managed Mongo clusters) is billed by compute tier (vCores / M-series such as M30 etc.) and storage; it does not charge by RUs. Request Units are the Cosmos DB (RU) model used for Cosmos DB (NoSQL / RU-based) accounts, not the vCore DocumentDB offering.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Plan and manage costs for Azure Cosmos DB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed the classic Cosmos RU model with the newer vCore (M-series) cluster model; both live under the Microsoft.DocumentDB namespace in different forms, causing memory confusion.

confusion_sources.title: Request Units in Azure Cosmos DB

confusions.build_risk: Using RU assumptions (or RU-based guidance) will mislead capacity sizing, cost estimates, and index tuning recommendations for the vCore cluster; code that auto-scales to RUs would not be applicable.
improvements: Add a short 'Billing model' callout to the top of the DocumentDB overview and to the agent-kit 'pricing guidance' page: 'DocumentDB (vCore) is vCore+storage billed; Cosmos DB RU is a different model.'

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported: SCRAM (username/password), X.509, and AAD via SASL/OAuth (acquire token and present via SASL/OAUTHBEARER or PLAIN/$external). Mostly use username/password.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native database credentials (SCRAM) and Microsoft Entra ID authentication. Microsoft Entra ID auth uses OIDC flow with authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and authMechanismProperties (ENVIRONMENT:azure, TOKEN_RESOURCE:...). The official docs show examples for MONGODB-OIDC and registration of managed identities; X.509 client-certificate auth is not the documented data-plane auth mechanism for DocumentDB clusters.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer included X.509 (a generic Mongo feature) and guessed SASL/OAUTHBEARER mechanics — the documented pattern for DocumentDB is MONGODB-OIDC with environment / token resource properties and portal-managed registration of identities.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming X.509 or an unsupported SASL plugin would produce authentication failures; implementing an incorrect Entra flow would prevent the app from connecting with managed identities.
improvements: Add an explicit example on the Connect doc showing the exact connection string and authMechanismProperties for Managed Identity (MONGODB-OIDC) and a short code snippet per language to obtain tokens if needed.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo/motor). No service-specific data-plane SDK; management uses azure-mgmt-cosmosdb.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python, MongoClient) for application data-plane code. Management/control-plane uses Azure management SDKs. The official quickstarts use pymongo and examples show MongoClient connecting to the cluster.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: DiskANN, HNSW and IVF supported. Example: db.tickets.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_idx', vector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', efConstruction: 200, m: 16 } })
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB supports vector-ivf, vector-hnsw and vector-diskann (IVF, HNSW, DiskANN). Indexes are created via a createIndexes/runCommand style that sets key to cosmosSearch and includes cosmosSearchOptions (kind: vector-hnsw|vector-ivf|vector-diskann) with parameters (dimensions, similarity, m, efConstruction, numLists, lBuild, maxDegree, etc.). Query is performed via $search with cosmosSearch vector options.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (DiskANN)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer named the correct algorithms but gave a non-DocumentDB index-creation snippet (generic Mongo-style); DocumentDB expects createIndexes with cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions instead of embedding:'vector' key shorthand.
confusions.build_risk: Attempting to create the index with incorrect options or the wrong command syntax will fail; the builder must use the cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions structure and set dimensions to match the embedding model.
improvements: Document a minimal example of createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions in the agent-kit quickstart and include a sample Python snippet that calls the data-plane MCP create index tool.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the service's integrated search or Azure Cognitive Search; combine text $search and vector kNN in application code; if $search exists you can combine.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB includes an integrated $search aggregation stage via cosmosSearch and integrated text + vector/hybrid ranking (the $search/cosmosSearch stage supports vector queries and lexical options). You can prefilter or combine text & vector in a single $search/cosmosSearch pipeline stage; using an external Azure Cognitive Search is an option but not required.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB
Full text search and hybrid search (agent skill doc)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described an older/common architecture (external Azure Cognitive Search or application-level merge) instead of the built-in hybrid `$search` capabilities DocumentDB now exposes.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses an external search service unnecessarily, they add complexity and cost; if they assume hybrid-search isn't native they may implement less accurate/performant merges.
improvements: Include an example on the quickstart that shows a single $search pipeline combining vector and text criteria and projecting searchScore so sample code demonstrates hybrid search directly.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supports MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol (per sample). Most driver functionality works but some server-side/admin features may be limited.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0 through 8.0 (the service advertises support for 5.0–8.0 depending on cluster serverVersion). Many application-facing features are supported (99.03% operator coverage), but some admin commands and server-only features are managed by the service and may not be directly exposed.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Run a local MongoDB docker image (mongo:7.0) on port 27017.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB provides a Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) that exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260; the agent-kit local-deployment guidance recommends using the Gateway image on 10260 and specific TLS/SCRAM settings to match production parity. Using a plain mongo:7 image is workable for basic driver compatibility but does not mirror DocumentDB-specific features (vector search, indexing extensions, ports and TLS setup).

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment
Query from any node in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Generic Mongo local-development advice uses the official mongo image on 27017; DocumentDB provides a Gateway image to mimic service features and default ports (10260).
confusions.build_risk: Testing only against mongo:27017 may hide differences in TLS requirements, port behavior, or vector-index features; the sample's seed and index commands may not work against plain mongo.
improvements: Add a one-paragraph Local Setup in the sample README: prefer DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (port 10260) for parity; include a fallback note explaining the limitations of connecting to mongo:latest for quick dev-only tests.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are not universally supported on the Cosmos/Mongo-compatible endpoint; Cosmos DB exposes Change Feed API; if Mongo change streams are available you must have a replica-set/cluster topology.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB-style change streams (including multi-shard change streams with a preview feature to enable). For multishard clusters you may need to enable the 'Change streams for multishard clusters' feature in the portal; change streams are supported and Azure provides documentation and examples for using watch()/aggregate($changeStream).

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Change streams in Azure Cosmos DB's API for MongoDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer defaulted to Cosmos DB's change feed vs Mongo change streams; DocumentDB explicitly supports Mongo change streams and has configuration requirements for multishard streams.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams don't exist would cause the builder to implement a polling or migration workaround unnecessarily; assuming they are available cluster-wide without enabling feature or verifying tier may cause runtime errors.
improvements: Add a short 'Change streams' note in the Quickstart that says: 'Mongo change streams are supported; enable multishard change streams in Features for multishard clusters.'

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the `documentdb` MCP server for this service. The general Azure MCP server handles management plane; use documentdb MCP for data-plane.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane commands (list databases, list indexes, create index, explain, find, aggregate). Azure MCP handles control-plane and documentation; both are useful but documentdb MCP is required for data-plane verification.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft had a service called Azure DocumentDB which later evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. Today Cosmos DB is umbrella; DocumentDB is legacy. Cosmos DB implements multiple APIs and Mongo API exposes wire compatibility but the underlying engine is Cosmos DB, not stock MongoDB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly incorrect: The product historically labelled 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' has been renamed to Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) in the recent documentation; Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is a distinct offering from Cosmos DB (RU) and is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (not the Cosmos proprietary storage engine). The old 'Azure DocumentDB' name (2014–2017) preceded Cosmos DB and that historical naming contributes to confusion; the current DocumentDB product is distinct and aligned with an open-source DocumentDB engine.

grounding_links.title: Frequently asked questions about Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)
DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple renames and overlapping brand names (DocumentDB → Cosmos DB → Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) → DocumentDB) have created a tangle; models often say 'Cosmos DB' when they mean the older DocumentDB account resource.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder follows older 'Cosmos DB' instructions for the vCore product they may provision the wrong resource or use incorrect connection/ billing assumptions.
improvements: Add a short timeline callout on the overview page and in the agent-kit: 'Which name to use when' clarifying differences between Cosmos DB (RU), DocumentDB (vCore), and the historic DocumentDB → Cosmos renaming.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underlying engine is the Cosmos DB implementation (Microsoft-managed), exposing a MongoDB wire protocol. Use standard drivers but expect subtle differences.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed by LF) built on PostgreSQL and provides a MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility layer. Applications use standard MongoDB drivers and most code will work, but there are subtle compatibility differences; testing is recommended.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The product family names (Cosmos DB vs DocumentDB) and presence of a Mongo wire-proxy create memory errors where agents attribute the engine to Cosmos rather than DocumentDB OSS.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a Cosmos DB engine under the hood may lead to incorrect assumptions about RU billing, index semantics, or migration paths.
improvements: Add an 'Engine and compatibility' section in the top-level README explaining that DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine and what that implies for compatibility vs Cosmos DB (RU).

confusions.question: How should the sample code obtain the cluster connection string at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI.
confusions.grounded_answer: Confirm: sample-run environment instructs the connection string be read from DOCUMENTDB_URI; the documentdb-local-deployment and quickstarts recommend using env-driven configuration and not committing secrets.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.question: Which database must the sample use for all created objects?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named `sample_customer_360_10` for everything the sample creates.
confusions.grounded_answer: Confirmed by the provided run-environment instructions in the sample prompt and supported by the quickstarts' pattern to use a single test database; the sample must use the database `sample_customer_360_10`.

grounding_links.title: Sample run environment (prompt)

confusions.question: What vector field name and dimensionality will the sample assume for embeddings?
confusions.cold_answer: Assume vector field named `embedding` and embeddings 1536-dimensional by default.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly true: the field name `embedding` is a reasonable and documented default; DocumentDB vector indexes require the correct `dimensions` that must match the chosen embedding model (DocumentDB supports large dims up to 16,000 for DiskANN). The docs show examples using 1536 dims but do not mandate it — dimension must match the embedding service chosen by the builder.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (index dimensions and example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: 1536 is a common embedding dimension (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small/etc.) but the service supports many dims and the sample must pick a model and set the index dimensions accordingly.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder creates a vector index with the wrong dimensions (e.g., 1536 while chosen embedding outputs 1536? OK; but mismatch leads to indexing/search failures), vector indexing will fail or return no results.
improvements: Make the embedding model and dimension explicit in the prompt or sample README (e.g., 'sample chooses OpenAI text-embedding-3-small (1536 dims); change DIM in config to match your provider').

confusions.question: Which client libraries will the sample use to implement a Python LlamaIndex RAG agent against this DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Use pymongo for Mongo connectivity and LlamaIndex (llama_index) for the RAG pipeline.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct as a valid choice: quickstarts and guidance use pymongo for connectivity; LlamaIndex is appropriate for RAG orchestration. The builder must also choose an embedding provider and LLM provider (OpenAI/Azure OpenAI/other) and include their clients in requirements.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python
Build RAG applications (LlamaIndex guidance)

confusions.question: Which MCP command will you use to inspect the collections and indexes from the `documentdb` MCP server profile `default`?
confusions.cold_answer: Use documentdb MCP tool: mcp documentdb collections list --profile default --database sample_customer_360_10 and documentdb indexes list ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct in intent: the documentdb MCP server exposes list and index commands (documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_get_statistics, documentdb_explain_operation) and the inventory shows those tools are available; use the MCP documentdb tools with connection_profile 'default'.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server tools (inventory)
documentdb_list_databases

information_gaps.title: Embedding model and dimension selection
information_gaps.description: No installed skill or documented repo file mandates which embedding model (provider + model name) the sample must use. The docs recommend matching vector index dimension to the embedding output, but they do not prescribe a default provider or model. Where I looked: LlamaIndex docs are not present in the installed skills; Microsoft docs show index dimension must match embeddings but do not pick a model.

information_gaps.title: LlamaIndex → DocumentDB vector store adapter details
information_gaps.description: No explicit documentation found in the installed skills or Microsoft docs about a maintained LlamaIndex adapter that writes embeddings into DocumentDB collections using cosmosSearch index definitions. The builder needs to choose or implement a minimal adapter mapping LlamaIndex document objects to Mongo documents with an 'embedding' number[] field and metadata; I searched the agent skills and Microsoft Learn docs for an out-of-the-box adapter and found none.

information_gaps.title: Pinned dependency set and reproducible requirements
information_gaps.description: The prompt review and installed skills do not specify an exact requirements.txt with pinned versions for pymongo, llama_index, or the OpenAI/Azure-OpenAI SDKs. The run environment only assures pip/virtualenv are available; builders must choose exact package versions to avoid runtime incompatibilities.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource (or az documentdb mongocluster CLI) for vCore DocumentDB clusters; do not attempt to provision the service with Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts when you intend a vCore mongo cluster.

Connect with mongodb+srv:// against <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (or <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com), enable TLS, and if using Microsoft Entra ID use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and the authMechanismProperties recommended in the docs.

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

guidance_for_builder.instruction: When creating a vector index, use createIndexes with cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions (kind: vector-hnsw | vector-ivf | vector-diskann) and set `dimensions` to exactly match your chosen embedding model; create a standard filter index on any prefilter fields.

sources.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and never write the secret into source control; provide a .env.example with a placeholder.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample; azd accelerates Azure template-based app provisioning but run environment already supplies a cluster and az is available. If you want azd-based workflows, install Azure Developer CLI via package manager (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/developer/azure-developer-cli/install).

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Bicep is useful for infra-as-code but not required to build the sample; if the repo includes Bicep samples, install Bicep CLI (az bicep install) or use az cli's built-in bicep support. The agent-kit or README should note that Bicep is optional for this sample and show az CLI alternatives.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Terraform is not needed for a code sample that uses an existing cluster; if Infra as Code is required add Terraform/AzAPI support in CI. For now document how to use az CLI or Bicep to inspect resources instead.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for a Python sample; add only if you want C# examples.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Having mongosh on PATH materially helps manual verification and debugging of collections and indexes; install the MongoDB Shell (mongosh) so developers can run ad-hoc queries against the cluster, or document how to use the documentdb MCP tools when mongosh is absent.
